title: Line 9 Hell Train
description:
Rush-hour express on Line 9.
Crammed between bodies, your feet lift slightly off the floor.

"The next station is..." Nobody can get off, and more pile on.
Your bag is crushed, no free hand for your phone.

choices.text: Endure it — this is part of the commute too
choices.result_text:
By the time you reached the office you were already drained.

If a foreign friend filmed this, they'd say 'unbelievable' —
But to a Korean office worker it's just Tuesday. A day's energy spent before work even starts.

choices.text: Let one train go and take the next
choices.result_text:
Let one train pass. The next was packed too, but a little better.

Decided to be two minutes late rather than be crushed.
Sometimes those two minutes save the whole day's sanity.

title: A Lap on a Ttareungi
description:
Ttareungi, Seoul's public bike share.
Scan the QR in the app, a thousand won an hour. Pull a bike from the rack.

The weather's good. Push the pedals and the wind picks up.

choices.text: Ride the Han River bike path
choices.result_text:
Rode along the Han River. Wind, glittering water, shade under the bridges.

No freedom like it for a thousand won.
While you're pedaling, even the 3 billion and the deadline fall behind you.

choices.text: Commute by bike to save the bus fare
choices.result_text:
Biked to work. Saved the fare and got some exercise.

Broke a little sweat, but better than subway hell.
Small savings and small freshness like this balance out a grinding day.

title: At the Community Center
description:
At the dong (neighborhood) community center to register my address.
Take a number and wait. Resident registration, fixed-date stamp, move-in report...

[The fixed-date stamp, called Hwakjeong Ilcha in Korean, is a 600 won legal stamp that records the exact date of your lease at the community center. If your landlord goes bankrupt or disappears, this stamp is what legally protects your deposit in foreclosure proceedings. Without it, you're last in line to get your money back. Thousands of Koreans have lost their entire jeonse deposits (sometimes 100 million won+) for skipping this one step.]

The clerk kindly walks me through each one.

choices.text: Handle it all properly — including the fixed-date stamp
choices.result_text:
Filed the move-in report and got the fixed-date stamp.
It's the first step to protecting a jeonse deposit — skip it and you can get burned later, I learned.

Learned one more grown-up task. Surviving in Seoul is the sum of paperwork like this.

choices.text: Do the essentials quickly and leave
choices.result_text:
Just filed the move-in report; I'll get the fixed-date stamp another time.

Knowing full well 'another time' is dangerous. But today I was worn out from waiting on a number.

title: The Parcel Locker
description:
The package you ordered yesterday is already in the parcel locker.
Punch in the code from the text and a compartment clicks open.

Korean delivery is fast. Ordered last night, here this morning.

choices.text: Open the package — a small thrill
choices.result_text:
Even for some mundane daily necessity, there's that little thrill of opening a package.

Fast delivery is one of the things foreign friends are most amazed by in Korea.
'How does it come next day?' Well — that's just Korea.

Wrong size, so you requested a return. Free return, picked up at the door.

When even returns are this easy, you keep buying.
Convenience always has its eye on your wallet — you shouldn't forget that.

title: Recycling Night
description:
Sunday night, recycling.
Plastic, cans, paper, vinyl, styrofoam, food waste...

Peel the labels, rinse, sort.
The very thing foreigners new to Korea say confuses them most.

choices.text: Sort it all carefully, by the rules
choices.result_text:
Peeled the PET-bottle labels, rinsed them, put them out separately.
The lady next door said 'well done' as she passed.

Maybe this small order is part of what keeps Korea running.
An invisible promise — everyone keeps it, so you do too.

choices.text: Bundle it loosely and head back in
choices.result_text:
Too tired, so you bundled it loosely.
The building guard probably re-sorted it the next day.

Felt a little guilty. You know there's convenience that runs on someone else's labor.
